units.title: Matter and Measurement
units.blurb: Sort matter, tell physical changes from chemical ones, and measure with the right units and digits.

units.title: Atoms and Isotopes
units.blurb: What atoms are made of, how we found out, and how atoms of one element can differ.

units.title: Electrons in Atoms
units.blurb: Energy levels, light from atoms, orbitals and electron configurations.

units.title: The Periodic Table
units.blurb: Read the table's layout and explain its trends from charge and distance.

units.title: Bonds, Formulas and Names
units.blurb: How atoms bond, how to write and name compounds, and what shapes molecules take.

units.title: Forces Between Particles
units.blurb: Explain melting points, boiling points and other bulk properties from the forces between particles.

units.title: The Mole
units.blurb: Count particles by weighing them, and find formulas from masses.

units.title: Chemical Reactions
units.blurb: Write, balance and classify reactions, and predict their products.

units.title: Stoichiometry
units.blurb: Use balanced equations to predict how much reacts and how much forms.

units.title: Gases
units.blurb: Explain gas behavior with moving particles, and predict it with the gas laws.

units.title: Solutions
units.blurb: How things dissolve, how much can dissolve, how to state concentration, and what happens when solutions mix.

units.title: Acids and Bases
units.blurb: Define acids and bases, measure them with pH, and neutralize them.

units.title: Energy and Change
units.blurb: Heat and temperature, specific heat, phase changes, and the energy of reactions.

units.title: Reaction Rates and Equilibrium
units.blurb: Why reactions speed up or slow down, and why some stop changing without stopping.

units.title: Nuclear Chemistry
units.blurb: Changes in the nucleus: radioactive decay, half-life, fission and fusion.

topics.title: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
topics.short: Pure substances have a fixed makeup; a mixture's makeup can vary.
topics.trouble: Students call a compound a mixture of its elements, or call salt water a pure substance because it looks the same all the way through.

topics.title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
topics.short: Particles move in every state; the states differ in how close the particles are and how freely they move.
topics.trouble: Students think the particles in a solid do not move at all, or that the particles themselves swell, melt or boil when heated.

topics.title: Physical and Chemical Changes
topics.short: A chemical change makes new substances; a physical change only changes form or state.
topics.trouble: Students call boiling or dissolving a chemical change because bubbles appear, or think every color change means a reaction.

topics.title: SI Units and Metric Prefixes
topics.short: Each prefix is a power of ten: 1 km = 10³ m and 1 mg = 10⁻³ g.
topics.trouble: Students move the decimal point the wrong way, writing 2.5 km = 0.0025 m, or mix up milli- (10⁻³) and micro- (10⁻⁶).

topics.title: Measurements and Significant Figures
topics.short: Read an instrument to one estimated digit, then count the digits that carry meaning.
topics.trouble: Students count leading zeros as significant, drop a meaningful trailing zero such as the one in 2.50 g, or report only the digits that have tick marks.

topics.title: Accuracy, Precision and Percent Error
topics.short: Accurate means close to the true value; precise means close to each other.
topics.trouble: Students think precise results must also be accurate, or divide by their own measured value instead of the accepted value when finding percent error.

topics.title: Significant Figures in Calculations
topics.short: Products and quotients keep the fewest significant figures; sums and differences keep the fewest decimal places.
topics.trouble: Students use the multiplication rule for sums, or round after every step instead of once at the end.

topics.title: Dimensional Analysis
topics.short: Multiply by conversion factors equal to 1, arranged so the units you do not want cancel.
topics.trouble: Students set a conversion factor upside down so nothing cancels, or convert cm³ to m³ by dividing by 100 instead of by 100³.

topics.title: Density
topics.short: Density is mass per unit volume; use it to find a mass, a volume or the identity of a substance.
topics.trouble: Students think a bigger or heavier object must be denser, or that cutting a block in half halves its density.

topics.title: Temperature Scales and Absolute Zero
topics.short: The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero: K = °C + 273.15.
topics.trouble: Students think 0 °C means no thermal energy at all, or that going from 10 °C to 20 °C doubles how hot something is.

topics.title: How We Learned What Atoms Are
topics.short: Dalton's atoms, Thomson's electrons and Rutherford's nucleus, each from an experiment.
topics.trouble: Students picture an atom as a solid ball, missing Rutherford's evidence that it is mostly empty space around a tiny, dense nucleus.

topics.title: Protons, Neutrons and Electrons
topics.short: The number of protons, the atomic number, decides which element an atom is.
topics.trouble: Students think the number of neutrons or electrons decides the element.

topics.title: Isotopes and Mass Number
topics.short: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons; mass number = protons + neutrons.
topics.trouble: Students find the neutrons by adding the atomic number to the mass number, or think isotopes of one element have different numbers of protons.

topics.title: Ions and Charge
topics.short: An atom that gains electrons becomes a negative ion; one that loses electrons becomes a positive ion.
topics.trouble: Students think a positive ion gained protons, or that losing electrons makes an atom negative.

topics.title: Average Atomic Mass
topics.short: The mass on the periodic table is the average of the isotopes' masses, weighted by how common each one is.
topics.trouble: Students average the isotope masses without weighting by abundance, or think some atoms have exactly the average mass.

topics.title: Energy Levels and Shells
topics.short: Electrons fill levels of rising energy: 2, then 8, then 8 for the first 20 elements.
topics.trouble: Students give potassium the shells 2, 8, 9 instead of 2, 8, 8, 1, or picture electrons circling the nucleus on fixed tracks like planets.

topics.title: Bright-Line Spectra
topics.short: An electron that drops to a lower level gives off light of one exact energy, so each element shows its own set of colors.
topics.trouble: Students think an atom can give off light of any energy, or that a bigger drop gives a longer wavelength when it gives a shorter one.

topics.title: Sublevels and Orbitals
topics.short: Level n has n sublevels (s, p, d, f), and each orbital in a sublevel holds at most two electrons.
topics.trouble: Students picture an orbital as a path the electron travels, or think every level holds exactly 8 electrons.

topics.title: Electron Configurations
topics.short: Fill sublevels in order of energy, read straight off the blocks of the periodic table.
topics.trouble: Students fill 3d before 4s by following the level numbers instead of the table's blocks, or write superscripts that do not add up to the number of electrons.

topics.title: Groups, Periods and Families
topics.short: Elements in a column have the same number of outer electrons and behave alike; each row starts a new shell.
topics.trouble: Students think the table is ordered by atomic mass, or mix up groups (columns) with periods (rows).

topics.title: Valence Electrons and Dot Symbols
topics.short: Count the outer-shell electrons of a main-group atom from its group and draw them as dots.
topics.trouble: Students count all of an atom's electrons instead of the outer ones, or give sulfur in group 16 sixteen valence electrons.

topics.title: Atomic Radius
topics.short: Atoms get bigger down a group as shells are added, and smaller across a period as more protons pull on the same shell.
topics.trouble: Students expect atoms to grow across a period because they have more electrons, missing the stronger pull of more protons on the same shell.

topics.title: Ionization Energy
topics.short: It takes more energy to remove an electron that is closer to more protons.
topics.trouble: Students explain the trend by saying atoms "want" a full shell, instead of reasoning from the nuclear charge and the distance.

topics.title: Electronegativity
topics.short: Electronegativity measures how hard an atom pulls on shared electrons; it rises up and to the right.
topics.trouble: Students give the noble gases the highest electronegativity, or confuse electronegativity with the number of valence electrons.

topics.title: Predicting Ion Charges
topics.short: Main-group atoms gain or lose electrons to match the nearest noble gas.
topics.trouble: Students predict that sodium gains seven electrons instead of losing one, or write the sulfide ion as S²⁺.

topics.title: Ionic Bonds
topics.short: Metals give electrons to nonmetals, and the oppositely charged ions hold each other in a lattice.
topics.trouble: Students picture table salt as separate NaCl molecules instead of a lattice in which every ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge.

topics.title: Formulas of Ionic Compounds
topics.short: Choose the ratio of ions that makes the total charge zero.
topics.trouble: Students cross the charges the wrong way and write Mg₂Cl for magnesium chloride, or leave Ca₂O₂ unreduced instead of writing CaO.

topics.title: Naming Ionic Compounds
topics.short: Name the metal, then the nonmetal ending in -ide; add a Roman numeral for metals with more than one charge.
topics.trouble: Students use prefixes such as di- for ionic compounds, or leave out the Roman numeral for iron and copper.

topics.title: Polyatomic Ions
topics.short: Groups such as NO₃⁻ and SO₄²⁻ act as single ions; use parentheses when you need more than one.
topics.trouble: Students drop the parentheses and write CaNO₃₂, or change a subscript inside the polyatomic ion to balance the charge.

topics.title: Covalent Bonds
topics.short: Nonmetal atoms share pairs of electrons in single, double or triple bonds.
topics.trouble: Students say atoms bond because they "want" eight electrons, instead of because the shared electrons are attracted to both nuclei.

topics.title: Naming Molecular Compounds
topics.short: Use prefixes to count atoms: N₂O₄ is dinitrogen tetroxide.
topics.trouble: Students use prefixes for ionic compounds, or add mono- to the first element, as in monocarbon dioxide.

topics.title: Lewis Structures
topics.short: Count all the valence electrons, connect the atoms, then complete octets with lone pairs and multiple bonds.
topics.trouble: Students count the wrong total of valence electrons, especially for ions, or give carbon five bonds.

topics.title: Molecular Shapes (VSEPR)
topics.short: Electron groups around an atom spread as far apart as they can, and lone pairs help set the shape.
topics.trouble: Students ignore lone pairs and call water linear, or count a double bond as two electron groups.

topics.title: Polar and Nonpolar Bonds
topics.short: The bigger the electronegativity difference, the more unevenly the bonding electrons are shared.
topics.trouble: Students treat ionic and covalent bonds as two separate boxes with a sharp cutoff, instead of the ends of a range of uneven sharing.

topics.title: Polar and Nonpolar Molecules
topics.short: A molecule is polar when its bond dipoles do not cancel out.
topics.trouble: Students call CO₂ polar because its bonds are polar, missing that its two dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.

topics.title: Ionic, Molecular, Network and Metallic Solids
topics.short: The kind of particles and the forces between them explain melting point, hardness and conductivity.
topics.trouble: Students think a high melting point always means an ionic compound, missing network solids such as diamond, or that solid salt conducts electricity.

topics.title: Intermolecular Forces
topics.short: Dispersion forces, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds pull whole molecules toward each other.
topics.trouble: Students think boiling water breaks the O–H bonds inside each molecule, instead of pulling whole molecules apart.

topics.title: Predicting Boiling Points
topics.short: Stronger forces between molecules mean a higher boiling point and a lower vapor pressure.
topics.trouble: Students rank boiling points by polarity alone, missing that large molecules have strong dispersion forces.

topics.title: The Mole
topics.short: A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, a count chosen so that a mole of atoms has a mass in grams equal to its atomic mass.
topics.trouble: Students think a mole of any substance has the same mass, or confuse a mole with a molecule.

topics.title: Molar Mass
topics.short: Add up the atomic masses in a formula to get the mass of one mole in grams.
topics.trouble: Students forget to multiply by a subscript, or by the 2 outside the parentheses in Ca(NO₃)₂.

topics.title: Grams, Moles and Particles
topics.short: Divide a mass by the molar mass to get moles; multiply moles by Avogadro's number to count particles.
topics.trouble: Students multiply by the molar mass when going from grams to moles, or mix up moles of molecules with moles of atoms.

topics.title: Percent Composition
topics.short: Each element's share of a compound's molar mass, as a percent.
topics.trouble: Students use the number of atoms instead of their masses, so they give water as 67% hydrogen.

topics.title: Empirical Formulas
topics.short: Turn masses into moles, then into the simplest whole-number ratio.
topics.trouble: Students round a ratio such as 1 : 1.5 to 1 : 2 instead of doubling it to 2 : 3, or use the mass ratio as if it were the mole ratio.

topics.title: Molecular Formulas
topics.short: A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, found from the molar mass.
topics.trouble: Students think the empirical formula is always the real formula, so they give glucose as CH₂O.

topics.title: Atoms Are Conserved
topics.short: In a reaction atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same.
topics.trouble: Students think mass is lost when wood burns or a gas escapes, because they do not count the gases that leave.

topics.title: Coefficients and Subscripts
topics.short: Subscripts say what one molecule is made of; coefficients say how many molecules there are.
topics.trouble: Students read 2H₂O as one molecule with four hydrogen atoms, or count the atoms in 3Ca(OH)₂ without multiplying through.

topics.title: Balancing Equations
topics.short: Change coefficients, never subscripts, until every element has the same count on both sides.
topics.trouble: Students change subscripts to balance an equation, which turns the substances into different ones.

topics.title: Types of Reactions
topics.short: Synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement and combustion.
topics.trouble: Students sort by surface pattern alone, missing combustion when the fuel contains oxygen, or calling every reaction of two compounds a double replacement.

topics.title: Predicting Single Replacements
topics.short: A more active metal replaces a less active one in a compound; the activity series tells which is which.
topics.trouble: Students think any metal can replace any other metal in a compound.

topics.title: Mole Ratios
topics.short: The coefficients of a balanced equation give the ratio of moles that react and form.
topics.trouble: Students use the subscripts or the masses as the ratio instead of the coefficients.

topics.title: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry
topics.short: Go from grams of one substance to moles, across the mole ratio, then back to grams of another.
topics.trouble: Students apply the coefficient ratio straight to grams, skipping the trip through moles.

topics.title: Limiting Reactant
topics.short: The reactant that runs out first decides how much product can form.
topics.trouble: Students pick the reactant with the smaller mass, or the smaller number of moles, without comparing to the coefficient ratio.

topics.title: Theoretical and Percent Yield
topics.short: Compare the product you actually got with the most the limiting reactant allows.
topics.trouble: Students divide the theoretical yield by the actual yield, or find the theoretical yield from the reactant in excess.

topics.title: Gas Pressure
topics.short: Pressure is the push of particle collisions on each square meter of wall, measured in atm, kPa or mmHg.
topics.trouble: Students think gas pressure pushes only downward, or that gas particles settle at the bottom of their container.

topics.title: Kinetic Molecular Theory
topics.short: The particles of a gas move fast and randomly, and the kelvin temperature measures their average kinetic energy.
topics.trouble: Students think every particle in a gas moves at the same speed, or that the particles stop moving at 0 °C.

topics.title: Boyle's Law
topics.short: At constant temperature, squeezing a gas into half the volume doubles its pressure: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
topics.trouble: Students expect every gas relation to be direct, so they predict that more pressure means more volume.

topics.title: Charles's Law
topics.short: At constant pressure, a gas's volume is proportional to its kelvin temperature.
topics.trouble: Students use Celsius temperatures, so warming from 10 °C to 20 °C seems to double the volume.

topics.title: Gay-Lussac's Law and the Combined Gas Law
topics.short: At constant volume, pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature, and P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ joins all three laws.
topics.trouble: Students forget to convert to kelvins, or put the starting and final values on the wrong sides of the equation.

topics.title: Avogadro's Law and Molar Volume
topics.short: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of particles: 22.4 L per mole at 0 °C and 1 atm.
topics.trouble: Students think a mole of a heavy gas takes up more room than a mole of a light gas at the same temperature and pressure.

topics.title: The Ideal Gas Law
topics.short: PV = nRT connects the pressure, volume, moles and temperature of a gas.
topics.trouble: Students use a value of R that does not match their units, or forget to change °C to K and mL to L.

topics.title: Why Things Dissolve
topics.short: Water's polar molecules pull ions and polar molecules apart and surround them: like dissolves like.
topics.trouble: Students think dissolved sugar has disappeared or turned into water, or that dissolving is the same thing as melting.

topics.title: Solubility and Solubility Curves
topics.short: A solubility curve shows the most solute that dissolves at each temperature.
topics.trouble: Students think every solute, gases included, dissolves better in hotter water, or call any solution with a lot of solute saturated.

topics.title: Molarity
topics.short: Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution.
topics.trouble: Students divide by the volume of water added instead of the final volume of solution, or use milliliters as if they were liters.

topics.title: Dilution
topics.short: Adding water spreads the same moles of solute through more volume: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
topics.trouble: Students think adding water changes the number of moles of solute.

topics.title: Precipitation and Solubility Rules
topics.short: Mixing two solutions can make an insoluble solid fall out, and solubility rules predict when.
topics.trouble: Students think every ionic compound dissolves in water, or give the precipitate a formula whose charges do not balance.

topics.title: Acids and Bases
topics.short: In water, acids make hydronium ions (H₃O⁺) and bases make hydroxide ions (OH⁻).
topics.trouble: Students think any compound with H in its formula is an acid, such as CH₄, or that any compound with OH is a base, such as the alcohol CH₃OH.

topics.title: Proton Donors and Acceptors
topics.short: An acid gives an H⁺ to a base, leaving a conjugate pair on each side of the equation.
topics.trouble: Students build a conjugate base by removing OH instead of H⁺, or think water can never act as an acid or a base.

topics.title: The pH Scale
topics.short: pH counts powers of ten: each step down the scale means ten times more H₃O⁺.
topics.trouble: Students think pH 3 is only a little more acidic than pH 4, missing the factor of 10.

topics.title: pH, pOH and the Ions in Water
topics.short: In water [H₃O⁺] × [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so pH + pOH = 14.
topics.trouble: Students think a basic solution has no H₃O⁺ at all, or that pure water contains no ions.

topics.title: Strong and Weak Acids
topics.short: A strong acid ionizes completely and a weak acid only partly; strength is not the same as concentration.
topics.trouble: Students confuse a strong acid with a concentrated one, and a weak acid with a dilute one.

topics.title: Neutralization
topics.short: An acid and a hydroxide base react to make water and a salt.
topics.trouble: Students think mixing any acid with any base gives pH 7, even when the moles of acid and base are not equal.

topics.title: Titration
topics.short: Add base drop by drop until it exactly uses up the acid, then work out the acid's concentration.
topics.trouble: Students use M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ for an acid such as H₂SO₄ that gives two H⁺, ignoring the 1 : 2 mole ratio.

topics.title: Heat and Temperature
topics.short: Temperature measures the particles' average kinetic energy; heat is energy that flows from hotter to colder.
topics.trouble: Students treat heat and temperature as the same thing, or think cold flows from a cold object into a warm one.

topics.title: Specific Heat
topics.short: q = mcΔT: some substances need more energy per gram to warm by one degree.
topics.trouble: Students think a substance with a high specific heat warms up faster, when it warms up more slowly.

topics.title: Calorimetry
topics.short: In an insulated cup, the heat lost by the hot object equals the heat gained by the cold one.
topics.trouble: Students drop the minus sign in q lost = −q gained, or pair the metal's mass with water's specific heat.

topics.title: Heating Curves and Phase Changes
topics.short: While a substance melts or boils, the added heat pulls particles apart and the temperature stays flat.
topics.trouble: Students think the temperature keeps rising while ice melts, or that boiling water gets hotter the longer it boils.

topics.title: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
topics.short: Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings; endothermic reactions take it in.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the system and the surroundings: a cold pack feels cold because the reaction takes heat from your hand, not because it gives off cold.

topics.title: Bond Energy and Reaction Energy
topics.short: Breaking bonds takes energy and forming bonds releases it; the difference is the energy change of the reaction.
topics.trouble: Students think breaking a bond releases energy, a widespread idea that has the energy flowing the wrong way.

topics.title: Collision Theory and Reaction Rate
topics.short: Particles must collide hard enough and lined up the right way, so temperature, concentration and surface area change the rate.
topics.trouble: Students think every collision makes a reaction, or that heating speeds a reaction only by causing more collisions, missing the larger share of collisions that are hard enough.

topics.title: Activation Energy and Catalysts
topics.short: A catalyst opens a path with a lower energy barrier and is not used up.
topics.trouble: Students think a catalyst gets used up, or that it changes how much energy the reaction releases.

topics.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
topics.short: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions run at equal rates, so the amounts stop changing.
topics.trouble: Students think the reactions stop at equilibrium, or that the reactants and products must be present in equal amounts.

topics.title: Le Chatelier's Principle
topics.short: A system at equilibrium shifts to partly undo a change in concentration, pressure or temperature.
topics.trouble: Students think adding a catalyst shifts an equilibrium, or that the shift undoes the change completely.

topics.title: Radioactive Decay and Nuclear Equations
topics.short: Alpha, beta and gamma decay change the nucleus, and both the mass numbers and the charges balance.
topics.trouble: Students think gamma decay changes the element, or balance the mass numbers and forget the atomic numbers.

topics.title: Half-Life
topics.short: In each half-life, half of the remaining nuclei decay; use it to find amounts left and ages.
topics.trouble: Students think a sample is all gone after two half-lives, taking away the same amount each time instead of halving what is left.

topics.title: Fission and Fusion
topics.short: Splitting heavy nuclei and joining light ones both release energy as a little mass disappears.
topics.trouble: Students mix up fission and fusion, or think the Sun runs on fission.
